scenarios.name: Setup: deck holds 36 cards (33 after the first round's 3 lots) and each of 4 seats takes a different contract from the pool of 6
Setup: every player starts with 6 coins and no goods (8 coins after one round's income with no purchases)
Each round draws 3 lots from the deck (36 -> 33)
Every player gains 2 coins in the round (6 -> 8 with no purchases)
Round 2 priority starts at seat 2: seat 2 buys Lot 1 at price 2 ahead of seat 1
Round 4 priority starts at seat 4: seat 4 buys Lot 1 at price 2 ahead of seat 1
Round 5 priority wraps back to seat 1: seat 1 buys Lot 1 at price 2 ahead of seat 4
Talk round happens and play continues normally (messages are answered automatically)
Limits range from 0 to 6: 0 and 6 offered, 7 never offered
Three positive limits: seat 1 buys only Lots 1 and 2, and Lot 3 goes to seat 2 at price 1
First offer is at price k=3 to the earliest queued seat in priority (seat 2)
Limit exactly equal to price 2 buys: seat 1 pays 2 and takes the good
Limits below price pass the offer down: the third queued seat buys at price 1
Too few coins passes the offer: seat 1 with 2 coins cannot pay 3, seat 2 buys at 2
Nobody queues: all three lots are discarded and nobody gains goods
Coins spent on Lot 1 count for Lot 2: seat 1 is then short and Lot 2 goes to seat 2 at price 1
After a lone purchase at price 1 the buyer's coins and goods are publicly updated
Game ends after round 12; all seats level at score 8 share the win
Final score: 10 coins + 2 own-colour goods + 3 other goods = 26
Game end reveals contracts and sets final scores (only scores are observable)
Tied score 15 is broken by more own-contract goods: seat 1 wins
Level on score and own-contract goods: seats 1 and 2 share the win

spec_choices.why: The designer chose 4, and the even rotation needs 12/N to be a whole number, which holds for 3 and 4. Three is the smallest table where two rivals contest a lot and the queue price ladder matters. Above 4, 6 contract colours and 3 lots per round get too thin. The strategy is to infer rivals' contracts from their purchases and talk, to bluff about your own, and to time your bids around the rounds where you hold priority.

spec_choices.what: Talk kept as a simultaneous poll broadcast to all
spec_choices.why: The source requires simultaneous messages. Players compete for lots and hide their contracts, so talk invites bluffing and deterrence that could cost a player who believes it.
own_goods is at most 6, which is below 100, so this ranks by score and then by own-contract goods. Players level on both share the win, which is the source's draw.
They are hidden during play and revealed only at the end; the score is the observable outcome.

simplifications.what: The three limits are collected as three consecutive simultaneous polls instead of one combined submission
simplifications.why: The engine takes one number per question. Limits are never revealed, so no player learns anything between the polls.

simplifications.what: The falling-price offer is unrolled into one conditional update per priority position for each lot
simplifications.why: The step list is flat. Up to N fixed steps with when/if conditions reproduce the sequential offer exactly.

simplifications.what: Final scoring and the contract reveal are a conditional update in round 12, just before the end check
simplifications.why: The score must be computed before the arithmetic ranking runs.

variation.original_summary: The Speicherstadt is a 2-5 player worker-placement auction. Players stack workers above revealed cards, the bottom worker may buy at a price equal to the stack height, and each decline drops the price by one for the next worker. Goods bought fill contracts or are sold, and the highest final total wins. The reviewed variation, Speicherstadt Queues, reduced this to 10 rounds of three one-good lots with secret contract colours, sealed price limits and a priority-ordered queue.

review.evidence: In the reviewed variation, no simple policy wins. Always pass ends on 26 coins and loses to anyone who buys a good at or below its value. Always bid 6 on lots 1 and 2 pays 3-4 for goods that are 80% likely worth 2, and it leaves Lot 3 cheap for others. Always bid 1 only buys when last in the queue. Seat order did build in an edge, though. Priority leader = ((r-1) mod N)+1 over 10 rounds gives seat 1 four leads and seats 2-3 three leads at N=3. At N=4, seats 1-2 lead 3 times and seats 3-4 lead twice. Each extra lead is worth about 2-4 points in games scoring 30-45.

Four skills separate players: setting limits by a good's value to you, spending 2 workers where queues will be short, buying to deny a rival's inferred colour, and hiding your own colour. All decks are equally supplied in each colour, so deal luck is limited to the order goods arrive.

A weak player who buys own-colour goods at 5 or less still scores above the pass baseline. A strong player keeps improving by reading queue and buy histories for rivals' colours, timing denial buys, and bluffing in talk.

Contract colours are hidden and limits are sealed. What each player queued for and bought is public, so rivals' colours must be inferred from behaviour. With 5 colours and 3-4 players, some colours belong to nobody, and spotting them is valuable.
Purchases follow from limits, coins and priority order by fixed rules. The score is coins + 5 per own-colour good + 2 per other good, and the winner is the higher score with an arithmetic tie-break.
The game uses sealed simultaneous numeric bids, one deck draw per round, simultaneous talk and 10 rounds. It has no board. The step count is about 12 per round.

problems: Seat edge: over 10 rounds the rotating priority leader gives some seats more lead rounds and more early-queue positions than others (N=3: 4/3/3; N=4: 3/3/2/2). Leading is worth about 2-4 points, so seat order alone skews results.
The rest of the priority order is also unbalanced: with 10 rounds, seats do not hold each queue position (2nd, 3rd, 4th) equally often, so the edge extends beyond the lead.
Allowing 2 players turns the higher-total rule into a pure difference contest, and 5 players cannot be made to rotate evenly through the round count.

changes.what: Play exactly 12 rounds with a 36-card deck: 6 colours (add Orange) × 6 cards each. Contracts are dealt from the 6 colours.
changes.why: 12 is a multiple of 3 and of 4. Under the rotation, each seat holds every priority position (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th) exactly 12/N times: 4 times each at N=3, 3 times each at N=4. Each colour still appears exactly 6 times, so every contract stays equally supplied.
changes.fixes: Seat edge: over 10 rounds the rotating priority leader gives some seats more lead rounds and more early-queue positions than others (N=3: 4/3/3; N=4: 3/3/2/2). Leading is worth about 2-4 points, so seat order alone skews results.

changes.what: The priority order each round is a full cyclic rotation starting from seat ((round-1) mod N)+1. It is stated as covering all positions, not just the leader.
changes.why: With 12 rounds the rotation is a complete set of cyclic shifts repeated 12/N times, so every seat has an identical distribution of queue positions.
changes.fixes: The rest of the priority order is also unbalanced: with 10 rounds, seats do not hold each queue position (2nd, 3rd, 4th) equally often, so the edge extends beyond the lead.

changes.what: Restrict the game to 3 or 4 players.
changes.why: With three or more players, one rival's gain is not another's loss, so the higher-total rule does not collapse into a difference contest. 12 rounds rotate evenly for both counts.
changes.fixes: Allowing 2 players turns the higher-total rule into a pure difference contest, and 5 players cannot be made to rotate evenly through the round count.

changes.what: Starting coins stay at 6 and income stays at 2 per round, so pass-only play reaches 30 coins. Limits stay 0-6.
changes.why: The price scale (1-4) against values (2 or 5) is unchanged, so the tested economics carry over. The 12th-round tie-break remains arithmetic.
changes.fixes: Seat edge: over 10 rounds the rotating priority leader gives some seats more lead rounds and more early-queue positions than others (N=3: 4/3/3; N=4: 3/3/2/2). Leading is worth about 2-4 points, so seat order alone skews results.

keeps: Workers queue on revealed goods, the first in the queue is offered the price equal to queue length, and each decline drops the price by 1 for the next worker.
Secret contract colour: own-colour goods are worth more than others.
Each player has a limited number of workers per round (2 for 3 lots), so placement is a real choice.
Coins plus goods value scoring, with the highest total winning.
A seasonal deck that runs out to end the game.

recommendation.reason: The queue auction with hidden contracts tests inference, denial and bluffing well. The only failure was a seat edge from an uneven rotation, which a 12-round, 36-card structure removes.

variation.name: Speicherstadt Queues (Even Rotation)
variation.summary: Players secretly hold a contract colour and queue workers on three goods per round. The first worker in each queue is offered the good at the queue's length, and the price falls by 1 with each decline. Over 12 rounds every seat holds every priority position equally often. Players infer rivals' colours from public queues and purchases, deny them, and bluff in simultaneous talk.
variation.rules:
SETUP: There are 6 colours: Red, Blue, Green, Yellow, Purple, Orange. The deck has 36 cards, 6 of each colour, shuffled once at the start. Each player is privately dealt a different contract colour, drawn at random from the 6 without repetition. No one else learns it. Each player starts with 6 coins and no goods. Players are numbered 1 to N (N = 3 or 4) in seating order.

The game lasts exactly 12 rounds. Each round:
1. SUPPLY: Reveal the top 3 cards of the deck as Lot 1, Lot 2 and Lot 3. Each lot is one good of the card's colour.
2. INCOME: Every player gains 2 coins.
3. PRIORITY: This round's priority order starts with player ((round - 1) mod N) + 1 and continues in seat order, wrapping around from N back to 1. It is announced. Over the 12 rounds every player holds each position in the priority order exactly 12/N times.
4. TALK: Everyone writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages are not binding and may be false.
5. QUEUE (secret, simultaneous): Each player submits three whole numbers, one per lot, each from 0 to 6.
   - A 0 means no worker on that lot.
   - A positive number places a worker there, and that number is the highest price the player will pay for that lot.
   - Each player has 2 workers, so at most 2 of the 3 numbers may be positive. If more than 2 are positive, only the positive entries on the two lowest-numbered lots count, and the rest become 0.
6. RESOLVE Lot 1, then Lot 2, then Lot 3:
   - The queue for a lot is every player with a positive number on it, ordered by this round's priority order. Let k be the queue length.
   - The offer starts at price k and goes to the first player in the queue.
   - If that player's limit is at least the current price and they hold at least that many coins, they pay that many coins to the bank and take the good.
   - Otherwise they decline, the price drops by 1, and the offer passes to the next player in the queue. The k-th player is therefore offered price 1.
   - If nobody buys, the card is discarded. A lot with an empty queue is discarded.
   - Coins spent on an earlier lot this round count when checking later lots.
7. ANNOUNCE: For each lot, announce which players queued, who bought it (if anyone) and the price paid. Limits are never revealed. Every player's coins and goods held (with colours) are public at all times.
8. END CHECK: After round 12 the deck is empty and the game ends.

FINAL SCORING: Each player's score is their coins, plus 5 points for each good of their own contract colour, plus 2 points for each good of any other colour. All contract colours are then revealed.
variation.objective: The player with the highest final score wins. If several tie for highest, the tied player with more goods of their own contract colour wins. If they are still tied, the game is a draw among them. If all players finish equal on both measures, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect:
Seat order no longer matters: every seat leads, and sits second, third and fourth, equally often, so differences in results come from play. The economics are unchanged from the tested version.
- A good worth 5 to you nets +1 to +4 at prices 4 to 1. A good worth 2 nets +1 at price 1, 0 at price 2, and a loss above that.
- Always pass ends on 30 and loses to any player who buys sensibly.
- Always bidding 6 on two lots overpays for goods worth on average 2.5 (1/6×5 + 5/6×2) and leaves the third lot cheap for others.
- Always bidding 1 only wins goods when last in the queue and is outscored by players who pay 2-4 for their own colour.
With 6 colours and 3-4 players, 2-3 colours belong to nobody. Identifying rivals' colours from their queues and buys, and denying them while hiding your own, is the core reasoning task.
Talk passes both tests. Players disagree because only one can win and each wants short queues on their own colour and long ones on rivals'. A player might claim a colour to scare others off a lot, or feign disinterest to buy cheaply. A player who simply follows a rival's suggestion ('I'll stay off Lot 2 if you stay off Lot 1') can be undercut when the rival queues anyway or was steering them away from the rival's own colour. They can also reveal their contract colour through what they agree to.
There is no endgame unravelling: the game is not about sustaining cooperation, and each round's purchases are independent value decisions.

balanced.evidence:
Value of a good: 5 if it is your contract colour, otherwise 2. The price offered is the queue length k minus the number of players ahead of you, so it runs from k down to 1, with k at most N (3 or 4). Net gain from a purchase = value minus price.

Net gain table (good worth 5 / good worth 2):
- price 1: +4 / +1
- price 2: +3 / 0
- price 3: +2 / -1
- price 4: +1 / -2

A worker costs nothing and a decline costs nothing, so the limit choice is close to truthful. Sensible play is to set the limit to 5 on your own colour and 1 or 2 on others, and to spend your 2 workers on the lots most likely to go cheap or matter most.

Thoughtless policies under the winner rule (other players sensible):
(a) Always pass (0,0,0): ends with 6 + 10x2 = 26 coins. Any sensible player buys at price at most value, so finishes at 26 or more and usually above. Pass loses.
(b) Always highest bid (6,6,x), which counts as lots 1 and 2 only:
- It never contests Lot 3, so a sensible player can usually take Lot 3 alone at price 1 (+1 or +4).
- When it is first in a 3 or 4 queue it pays 3-4 for a good that is 80% likely worth 2 (-1 or -2).
- Its expected value per good is 0.2x5 + 0.8x2 = 2.6, so at prices of 2 or more it gains about 0.6 or loses.
- Example, 3 players, 2 maximal bidders vs 1 sensible player: the bidders split lots 1 and 2 at price 2 each (about +0.6 each), while the sensible player takes Lot 3 at 1 (about +1.6) and can join the Lot 1 or Lot 2 queue when that lot is their contract colour, so the sensible player outscores both. The policy loses.
(c) Always queue the first two lots with the minimum limit 1: it only ever buys at price 1, does not dominate, and is beaten by a player who takes own-colour goods at 2-4. No option is strictly better whatever the opponents do.

Both or all players can win. The deck is exactly 30 cards (10 rounds x 3), so each colour appears exactly 6 times and every contract is equally supplied.

SEAT EDGE (fail): the priority leader is ((r-1) mod N)+1 over 10 rounds.
- N=3: seat 1 leads 4 rounds (1,4,7,10); seats 2 and 3 lead 3 each.
- N=4: seats 1 and 2 lead 3 rounds; seats 3 and 4 lead only 2.

Leading matters. On your own-colour lot, being first lets you buy at k before anyone else can deny you. If you are behind, a rival offered price 2 for a 2-point good can buy it at zero net cost and deny you a +3/+4 gain. Each extra lead round is therefore worth about 2-4 points in a game where scores are about 30-45. That is a built-in edge from seat order that does not vanish with skill.

playable.evidence:
Rules cover every case:
- The over-2-positive entries rule (keep the two lowest-numbered lots).
- An empty queue: the lot is discarded.
- Insufficient coins: the player declines.
- Coins spent on earlier lots count for later lots.
- The price falls by 1 per decline, ending at 1 for the k-th player.
- The tie-break: own-colour goods, then a draw.

The game is finite (10 rounds, deck exactly used up) and the score is pure arithmetic on coins and goods counts the engine keeps. Contract colours are hidden only from players; the engine scores with them.

Complexity is within limits:
- About 10 steps (20 max).
- 2 choice steps (talk and queue; 4 max).
- 11 attributes (20 max).
- 2 hidden elements (contract colours and simultaneous limits; 3 max).
- 1 random draw (the reveal of 3 cards from a pre-shuffled list, done with remove/append).
- 10 rounds (40 max).

Queue resolution with wrap-around priority is calc-heavy but arithmetic, and a referee can rule the per-lot step. There is no board, clock, trading or binding agreement. The queue is a simultaneous secret poll, as required.

Talk is simultaneous and justified: players compete for the same lots and have hidden colours, so claims ('I want Lot 2', 'my colour is Blue') can be bluffs that cost followers. It is not a fixed-length cooperation dilemma, and there is no last-round collapse: buying at price 1 or 2 stays worthwhile through round 10.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance comes from deck order: which round and which lot position your colour appears in, relative to your priority. The quantity of each colour is fixed at 6, so contract luck is removed. I estimate about 25-35% of outcome variance is timing luck.

Things to infer:
- Purchase prices are announced. A buy at price 3 or 4 almost certainly reveals a contract colour (it is a loss for a 2-point good).
- Queue membership reveals interest.

Ways to act on it:
- Deny a rival's colour by buying it at a price of 2 or less, at zero net cost.
- Avoid crowded queues, which pushes the price up for whoever is first.
- Pick uncontested lots for price-1 buys.
- Bluff in talk.

When everyone plays well, everyone reads colours and denies. The winner is then decided by how well each player anticipates queue lengths and denials across the 3 lots, not by the deal alone. All colours are equally supplied, so no dealt contract wins by itself. A reasoning player clearly beats a careless one: see policy (b), which loses about 1 point per round to sensible placement.

required_changes:
Remove the seat edge in priority:
- Make the number of rounds a multiple of both 3 and 4: 12 rounds with a 36-card deck of 6 colours x 6 cards (add Orange; contracts dealt from 6 colours), so each seat leads equally often for N=3 (4 each) and N=4 (3 each).
- Or keep 10 rounds and give priority each round to the player with the fewest coins (ties broken by fewest goods, then lowest seat number not yet having led), stated as an arithmetic rule.

balanced.evidence:
VALUES AND PRICES. A good of your own colour is worth 5 points and any other good is worth 2. Coins are worth 1 point each. The offer price on a lot starts at k (the queue length, at most N, and N is at most 4) and drops by 1 per decline. So the price is always between 1 and 4.

Net gain from accepting a good at price p:

| Good | p=1 | p=2 | p=3 | p=4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Own colour | +4 | +3 | +2 | +1 |
| Other colour | +1 | 0 | -1 | -2 |

Own-colour goods are always worth buying. Other-colour goods are worth buying only at price 1, or at price 2 as pure denial. Denial is the main tension. If an opponent ahead of you in the queue takes your colour at price 2, it costs them 0 net and costs you a 5-point good. Since the game is decided by relative score, denial matters.

Thoughtless policies, tested against the WINNER RULE:

(a) ALWAYS PASS. This ends with 6 + 24 = 30 points. A sensible player who buys around 4 own-colour goods at an average price of about 2 nets roughly +12, plus some +1 cheap goods, for about 42 or more. Always-pass loses against sensible play. Against random play (random limits on 2 lots) it sometimes wins, because random players overpay for off-colour goods at 3 or 4. It still loses whenever the random players happen to land on their own colour. It does not win almost every time.

(b) ALWAYS MAX: limit 6 on Lots 1 and 2. When this player is first in the queue it pays k. With N=4 and around 3 queuers that is 3 for a good worth 2.5 on average (1/6 chance of 5, 5/6 chance of 2), about breakeven or worse. It also ignores Lot 3 even when Lot 3 is its colour. It drains coins: income is 2 per round, so it is often broke for later lots. Sensible players let it overpay and then take their own colour. It loses regularly.

(c) ALWAYS LIMIT 1 ON TWO LOTS. It never overpays, but it only buys when it is last in the queue or everyone ahead declines. A sensible player bidding 5-6 on its own colour takes those lots first. Always-1 collects about +1 per scrap good and forfeits most of its own colour (+4 each). It loses to sensible play.

(d) ALWAYS LAST LOT / FIRST LOT. The positions of lots carry no fixed value, because colours are random. It is not dominant.

No option is strictly better regardless of the opponent. Bidding 2 or more on others' colours helps against one rival and hands points to the third player, so it depends on reading who leads.

SEAT EDGE. Priority rotates exactly, giving 4 times first each for N=3 and 3 each for N=4. All information is symmetric apart from each player's own colour. All 36 cards are revealed over the 12 rounds, so every colour supplies exactly 6 goods. Every player can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
The rules are complete:
- The deck size (36) matches 12 rounds × 3 lots, and the end is fixed at round 12.
- The queue order is the announced priority order.
- The price starts at k and decreases by 1, with explicit coin and limit checks.
- There is an explicit overflow rule for more than 2 positive bids.
- Earlier spending carries into later lots.
- Unbought and empty lots are discarded.
- Scoring and a two-level tiebreak end in a draw.

Everything is arithmetic on coins, goods and colours that the game keeps. There is no board, clock or judge.

Platform limits, all inside:
- steps 12 (limit 20)
- choice steps 2 (talk and queue; limit 4)
- attributes 14 (limit 20)
- hidden elements 2 (contract colour and limits; limit 3)
- random draws 1 (the deck reveal; limit 1)
- rounds 12 (limit 40)

The queue is a simultaneous poll, as required. Talk is simultaneous and sits where players disagree: who takes which lot, bluffing about colours, threats of denial. Following a proposal can cost you, for example by stepping off a lot that turns out to be yours. So talk is appropriate with 3-4 players.

This is not a cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply. Late rounds still carry real choices, because own-colour goods stay profitable at any legal price.

triage.reason: Both failures are 'never matched' complaints about Ada's scripted answers, not wrong coins, goods or scores. That fits a correct game that stops asking for a Lot 3 limit once a player has placed both workers on Lots 1 and 2. Under R8 such a player's Lot 3 entry would be forced to 0 anyway, so the game is right not to put the Lot 3 option to that seat, and the scripts expecting a third answer go unmatched.
triage.guidance: Do not script answers for a choice the rules make moot. Once a player has given positive limits on Lots 1 and 2, the game may skip the Lot 3 question, so do not require a Lot 3 answer (a 1 in R8, a 0 in R13) with a fixed 'times' count. Use non-strict counts or drop those rules. Test R8 through outcomes instead: after the round the player holds at most 2 new goods, their coins match paying only for Lots 1 and 2, and Lot 3 goes to the next queuer or is discarded. Test R13 through outcomes too: Ada spends her coins on Lot 1, is then too short to pay the Lot 2 price, and Lot 2 goes to the next player in the queue at the lower price. Check this in the players' coins and goods, not in how many prompts Ada received.
